<reason>Both sides were skilled and well-grounded, but B did more lasting damage to A's two central pillars. On feasibility, A's "decisive" pathway collapsed into voluntary recognition by conferences — which B cleanly exposed as the very unilateral authority A opened against, with the other routes (NLRB reversal, Congress, Southern statehouses) left speculative. On durability, B turned A1.5 twice: the bargained cap's antitrust immunity protects the cap rather than athletes, and without employee status a voluntary-recognition deal earns no labor exemption at all — a mechanistic hit A never repaired. B also answered both pressure questions directly and on-format, while A's "silence" charge was premature given B's answering speech came next in the chronology. A landed real blows — the "who holds the wrench" question, the setting-terms-vs-appealing-application frame, and an honest unit-definition answer — but its closing never returned to the feasibility and exemption damage. B's closing took A's own test ("representation means setting terms") and showed A's model failing it twice, giving the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 double-turn: A's decisive instrument (conference-level voluntary recognition) means the table exists only by the schools' unilateral permission, and a cap signed with non-employees gets no labor exemption — gutting the durability mechanism A had called "the point that should decide the round," with no repair in A's closing.</best_rebuttal>
